drills.q: Why did RAG exist before context windows got large?
drills.a: Early context windows (2K-16K tokens) couldn't fit a knowledge base at all, so retrieval was the only mechanism for exposing external knowledge to a model, not a design choice.

drills.q: What did 'Lost in the Middle' actually measure?
drills.a: Multi-document QA and key-value retrieval with the relevant document/fact placed at different positions in context, showing a U-shaped accuracy curve -- best at start/end, worst (20+ pp degradation in some configs) in the middle.

drills.q: A PM wants to remove the vector database because the new model has a 2M-token window. What do you ask first?
drills.a: What fraction of the corpus a typical query needs, query volume, how often the corpus updates, whether citations are needed, and the task shape (lookup vs multi-hop/aggregation) -- if most queries need a small slice, volume is high, and citations matter, keep RAG regardless of window size.

drills.q: Why doesn't NIAH benchmark performance generalize to real production accuracy?
drills.a: NIAH tests the easiest case: one unambiguous fact, simple factoid question, no cross-fact reasoning. Production questions are often multi-hop or require aggregation, where benchmarks like RULER show effective context length is shorter than advertised even for models that saturate NIAH.

drills.q: When does context caching fail to save money even though it's set up correctly?
drills.a: If query-specific content is inserted before the cacheable prefix, or the static portion gets reordered/personalized, the exact-prefix-match requirement breaks and every call becomes a full-price cache miss.

drills.q: How do you tell apart a RAG retrieval-recall failure from a long-context utilization failure?
drills.a: Check whether the correct information was actually present in the retrieved context/prompt at all. If yes and the model still got it wrong, that's a utilization (positional-attention) failure. If it was never surfaced, that's a retrieval recall failure -- different fixes follow.

drills.q: Design the retrieval strategy for a legal-document Q&A system where some queries need one clause and others need to reason across the whole contract.
drills.a: Route by query shape: single-clause lookups go through standard RAG (fast, cheap, precise); whole-contract risk-reasoning queries load the full contract into a long-context call, ideally cached if a session asks multiple follow-ups. Use a query classifier or cheap first-pass check to decide the route.

drills.q: Your team says removing RAG for long context improved eval accuracy. Do you trust it?
drills.a: Check whether the eval set is dominated by single-fact lookup (long context's saturated strength) versus multi-hop/aggregation, and whether the eval corpus size matches production scale. Without a task-shape-diverse, production-scale eval (ideally RULER-style, not just NIAH), the result doesn't generalize.
